lesson.title: The Same Signal, Viewed by Frequency Instead of Time
lesson.summary: The frequency domain represents a signal by the amplitude and phase of each frequency component it contains rather than by its value at each instant, the view a Fourier series or a spectrum analyzer provides.
lesson.body:
Some questions are almost impossible to answer from a time domain trace but nearly instant to answer once the same signal is reorganized by frequency. How much third harmonic distortion does this waveform have? Will this signal's harmonics interfere with a nearby radio band? How much filtering is needed to smooth this pulse train into clean DC? All of these are frequency domain questions, and the frequency domain is nothing more than the same signal's information, sorted by frequency instead of by time. Crucially, this is a reorganization, not new information: a Fourier series is invertible, meaning that if you know every an and bn you can reconstruct f(t) exactly, and if you know f(t) you can compute every an and bn. Time domain and frequency domain are two complete, equivalent views of one underlying signal.

The picture that represents the frequency domain view of a periodic signal is exactly the frequency spectrum from two chapters back: harmonic amplitude Cn plotted against frequency n f0. Where the time domain plot has a horizontal axis in seconds, the frequency domain plot has a horizontal axis in hertz, and where the time domain plot traces a continuous shape, the frequency domain plot for a periodic signal is a set of discrete lines, since energy only exists at the fundamental and its harmonics.

As a fully worked example, take the same square wave used in the last few chapters, 10 V peak, 1 kHz fundamental. Its time domain view is a flat topped waveform that switches abruptly between +10 V and -10 V every half period, the classic brick shape on a scope screen. Its frequency domain view, of the exact same signal, is a set of spectral lines at 1 kHz (12.73 V), 3 kHz (4.24 V), 5 kHz (2.55 V), and 7 kHz (1.82 V), with nothing at 2, 4, or 6 kHz. Both pictures describe the identical voltage waveform. You would reach for the time domain view to check timing margins or rise time; you would reach for the frequency domain view to check whether a filter needs to attenuate the third harmonic, or whether the signal will pass an electromagnetic interference test at a given frequency.

In practice, the conversion between the two views is done automatically. A digital oscilloscope's FFT (fast Fourier transform) function takes a captured time domain record and numerically computes the Fourier coefficients from it, displaying the result as a frequency domain trace on the same screen. Knowing what that FFT trace actually represents, the amplitude of each harmonic sitting at its own frequency, is what turns it from a mysterious extra button into a genuinely useful diagnostic.
